title: Smallest triangle-free 6-chromatic graph: is 40 vertices optimal?
credit: Problem of determining n(k): Jensen-Toft 'Graph Coloring Problems'; bounds J. Goedgebeur (JGT 2020); n(5)=22 Jensen-Royle (1995).
premise_risks: Largely computational (rule 5); accepted only because it is a recognised open problem with refereed bounds
The 40-vertex upper-bound graph should be double-checked as coming from the JGT paper (abstract states the 40 bound)
Thematically adjacent to board item QED-E056 (minimum-order k-chromatic graphs of girth >= g), but asks for a specific value n(6), not the girth question
plain: Triangle-free graphs can need arbitrarily many colours, but they must be large. The smallest triangle-free graph needing 4 colours has 11 vertices (the Grötzsch graph), and the smallest needing 5 colours has 22 vertices. For 6 colours, the smallest such graph is known to have between 32 and 40 vertices. Either find a triangle-free graph on at most 39 vertices that cannot be properly coloured with 5 colours, or prove that every triangle-free graph on 39 vertices is 5-colourable.
math: Let $n(k)$ be the minimum order of a triangle-free graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=k$. Known: $n(4)=11$, $n(5)=22$, $32\le n(6)\le 40$. Decide whether $n(6)=40$, i.e. whether every triangle-free graph on $39$ vertices satisfies $\chi(G)\le 5$.
